public-speaking-1: Public speaking is the designing and delivering of a message to an audience, and I defined rhetoric as observing the available means of persuasion in each case. Start with the conversation: a speaker and a listener who must decide something. Name the three purposes of a speech and the three parts of getting a message heard, and write one speech you might give with its purpose. The art begins with a question of who decides and about what, so ask it of your own speech.

A speaker's character carries weight with an audience, and in my account it is among the means of persuasion. Think about ethics from the start: your intent, your means and your ends. Ask whether you have been honest about your sources, fair to your audience and careful with your claims. Learn the three plagiarism traps and write how you will avoid each. A speech built on a borrowed idea you have not credited persuades no one for long once they find out.

Nerves are a normal response to being evaluated, and the body treats the audience as a threat. Learn the myths and the different kinds of anxiety, and write which ones you recognise in yourself. I separated the speaker's character, the audience's feeling and the proof in the speech, and nerves belong to the first two. Understanding what happens in your body is the first step to using the energy.

Anxiety tends to peak just before you start and then decline as you speak. Plan for the first minute, when you will feel it most, and for the unexpected: a lost note, a noisy room, a question you cannot answer. Prepare, practise and write down what you will do. Rehearse the opening until it is automatic, and the rest will follow.
public-speaking-2: Hearing is automatic, and listening is purposeful and takes effort. Understand what makes listening hard, and design the speech to help. I held that a speech is made of a speaker, a subject and a listener, and the listener decides its end. Write three things that will make your audience lose the thread, and one thing you will do about each. Keep the listener in mind from the first line.

Audience analysis is learning all you reasonably can about the people you will speak to. Use three kinds: who they are, what they believe and want, and the situation they are in. Avoid stereotypes, and take care not to offend. Remember that the kind of speech depends on who decides and about what: an assembly decides about the future, a court about the past. Write a short profile of a real audience using all three kinds.

When you survey or interview, keep your questions related to your topic, use a standard set, keep it short, say that it is voluntary, and ask at least ten to twenty people. Beware answers given to please. Use what you learn to change what you say, how you open and which examples you choose. Write what the information changed in your plan.

A general purpose is the broad goal: to inform, to persuade or to entertain. Narrow the topic using four constraints and a funnel, and then write a specific purpose statement that says what the audience will understand or do. Test it by asking whether it can be done in the time. A purpose that is too wide is a speech that never ends.
public-speaking-3: I held that a speaker should gather widely first and then choose. Plan your research time and your search, and keep a log of what you looked for and what you found. Primary research is reported by the person who did it, and secondary research reports other people's work. Gather more than you will use, then keep what supports your purpose. A log lets you find a source again and show that you have not made it up.

Judge a source by four tests: accuracy, authority, currency and objectivity. Popular sources are good for background, and academic sources go through review. Check who wrote it, when, and who paid. Where a source fails a test, say so. A speaker who knows the weakness of the evidence is believed more than one who hides it.

Support has three jobs: it clarifies, builds credibility and makes the speech vivid. Choose among facts and statistics, definitions, examples, narratives, testimony and analogy, and use more than one kind. Keep general arguments ready, and use them where they fit. Use statistics honestly, with the source and the date. Write which kind of support each of your main points will use.

Present each piece of evidence in three steps: setup, execution and analysis. Tell the audience the source's name, where it appears, the date and the expert's standing. Then give the evidence, and then explain what it shows for your point. Choose whether to quote, paraphrase or summarise, and check that you have enough. Hold your points in your memory by their order, and rehearse the steps aloud.
public-speaking-4: An introduction is only about 10 to 15 percent of the time, so a five-minute speech needs one of no more than 45 seconds. It has five jobs: gain attention, state the purpose, establish credibility, give reasons to listen and preview. I would have you open to make the audience willing, attentive and ready to learn. Write your introduction with those five jobs and time it.

The body is where the purpose is achieved. Brainstorm every point, then group them into two or three main points. Each point should do one job. Choose an organising pattern that suits the purpose, and test it by asking whether the order helps the listener. State the facts of your case clearly, briefly and credibly. Cut any point that does not serve the purpose.

Readers can re-read, and listeners cannot. Use transitions, internal previews, internal summaries and signposts to keep the audience with you. End so that the audience knows it has ended, with the point you want remembered. Rehearse the movement between the points as carefully as the points themselves. Say it plainly, and say it once more at the end.

An outline tests whether your speech holds together: scope against the thesis, the logic of the parts, the relevance of the support, and the balance. Write the full-sentence outline first, then reduce it to a speaking outline and notecards. Practise from the cards, not from a script. Test yourself without the cards, and mark the point where you lost the thread.
public-speaking-5: Spoken language came long before written language, and listeners hear words once. Choose the exact short word, and use language that is vivid, familiar and appropriate. Learn the difference between a word's plain meaning and what it suggests. I held that the short word is usually the right one. Rewrite one paragraph of your speech in the words you would say aloud, and read both versions.

Judge your words for the speaker, the audience, the context and the topic. Keep the language clear and economical, inclusive and confident. Cut jargon, filler and hedges that weaken your point. Build a climax from facts that all point one way. Read a page aloud and mark each word you stumbled on or did not mean. Replace those words.

Speaking is less formal than reading and more formal than talking. There are four methods of delivery, and each suits different occasions. Choose by the room, the time and the purpose, and plan for a lectern or a microphone. Practise in a room like the real one. I held that the power to speak is cultivated by practice, so give yourself the practice.

Delivery should be clear, interesting and undistracting, with the directness of conversation. The well-known figures on face, voice and words are often misquoted, so use them with care. Practise well: aloud, standing, with a timer, and with someone listening. Record yourself, and mark one thing to keep and one to change. Do it again, and compare.
public-speaking-6: Aids will not rescue a poor speech. Used well, they improve a good one by helping understanding, memory, interest and credibility. Choose the aid for the job: a chart for a trend, an object for a shape, a slide for a list. I opened with the question my audience avoided, and an aid should do the same kind of work: bring the point into view. Choose one aid for your speech and say which of the four jobs it does.

The people at the back must be able to see or hear any aid. A graphic should take about a third of the slide, with a little large, simple text. Print handouts for after the speech, and have a backup plan if the equipment fails. Test the room before you speak. Rehearse with the aid, and cut it if it distracts.

A good informative speech is accurate, clear and interesting. It exists to give listeners knowledge so that they can make up their own minds. On a controversial topic, give a fair statement of each side. I argued from what my audience already declared it believed, and an informative speech earns trust by starting there. Check each fact and give the source.

Persuasion is an attempt to change what a person thinks or does, in values, attitudes and beliefs. Choose whether to change a belief or a behaviour. Make a claim, give reasons and evidence, and answer the objection the audience will raise. Choose your tone on purpose: argument when it will work, and irony or fire when argument is not enough. Keep to the audience's own principles, and be honest about what you ask.
public-speaking-cap: The brief is a five-minute extemporaneous speech to inform or persuade a real audience of at least three people. Choose a topic you know or can research in a week, and use at least three sources judged for accuracy, authority, currency and objectivity. Write a full-sentence outline and five speaking cards. Build the climax from facts that all point one way. Plan the week so that you have time to rehearse twice.

Score the recording against the rubric, 0 to 4 on each criterion. A pass is 3 or more on every criterion, or 2 on one with a written plan to improve. Watch the recording twice, first for the whole and then for the parts. Write what you would change and what you would keep. Choose the exact short word where you used a long one. Practise again before the next speech.
